questions.problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{y}{4}=25\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

has the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
questions.worked_solution:
The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $25\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x,
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x)-(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡x)+\frac{\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x}{4}=25\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
(-\frac{3}{4}\alpha -\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡x+(\alpha -\frac{3}{4}\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡x=25\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{4}\alpha -\beta =25\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\ \alpha -\frac{3}{4}\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-12$ and $\beta =-16.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-12\operatorname{cos}⁡x-16\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the problem

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3y=2\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda -3 & =0 \\ (\lambda +3)(\lambda -1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =-3$ or $\lambda =1$, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-3x}+B{e}^{x}.
$$

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $2\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is 

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x,
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x)+2(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡x)-3(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
(2\beta -4\alpha )\operatorname{cos}⁡x+(-2\alpha -4\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}-4\alpha +2\beta =2\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\ -4\beta -2\alpha =1\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{1}{2},$ $\beta =0.$

Therefore, the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{-3x}+B{e}^{x}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+10y=\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+31\operatorname{sin}⁡3x.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+10y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +10 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +1)-1+10 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)^{2} & =-9 \\ \lambda +1 & =\pm 3\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-1\pm 3\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =-1\pm 3\text{i}$, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}={e}^{-x}(A\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡3x).
$$

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+31\operatorname{sin}⁡3x.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3x,
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡3x+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡3x \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =-9\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3x-9\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3x\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
(-9\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3x-9\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3x)+2(-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡3x+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡3x)+10(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+31\operatorname{sin}⁡3x
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
(\alpha +6\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+(-6\alpha +\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡3x=\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+31\operatorname{sin}⁡3x.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}\alpha +6\beta =1\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡3x) \\ -6\alpha +\beta =31\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡3x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-5$ and $\beta =1.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-5\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\operatorname{sin}⁡3x.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y={e}^{-x}(A\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡3x)-5\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\operatorname{sin}⁡3x.
$$

questions.problem:
Find the solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4y=13\operatorname{sin}⁡3x.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +4 & =0 \\ {(\lambda -2)}^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =2$ is a repeated root, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{2x}+Bx{e}^{2x}.
$$

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $13\operatorname{sin}⁡3x.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3x,
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡3x+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡3x \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =-9\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3x-9\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3x\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
(-9\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3x-9\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3x)-4(-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡3x+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡3x)+4(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3x)=13\operatorname{sin}⁡3x
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
(-5\alpha -12\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+(12\alpha -5\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡3x=13\operatorname{sin}⁡3x.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}-5\alpha -12\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡3x) \\ 12\alpha -5\beta =13\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡3x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =\frac{12}{13}$ and $\beta =-\frac{5}{13}.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\frac{12}{13}\operatorname{cos}⁡3x-\frac{5}{13}\operatorname{sin}⁡3x.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{2x}+Bx{e}^{2x}+\frac{12}{13}\operatorname{cos}⁡3x-\frac{5}{13}\operatorname{sin}⁡3x.
$$

questions.problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+9y=-6\operatorname{cos}⁡3x
$$

has the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡3x$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
questions.worked_solution:
The particular solution of the inhomogeneous equation cannot be of the form $\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3x$ because this is already included in the complementary function. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3x),
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3x)+3x(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡3x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡3x) \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =6(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡3x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡3x)-9x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3x)\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
6(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡3x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡3x)-9x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3x)+9x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3x)=-6\operatorname{cos}⁡3x
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
-6\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡3x+6\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡3x=-6\operatorname{cos}⁡3x.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}6\beta =-6\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡3x) \\ -6\alpha =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡3x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =0$ and $\beta =-1.$ Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-x\operatorname{sin}⁡3x.
$$

questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the  equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+4y=8\operatorname{cos}⁡2x-\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+4y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =\pm \text{2i}$, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}=P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.
$$

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$ 

The particular solution of the inhomogeneous equation cannot be of the form $\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2x$ because this is already included in the complementary function. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2x),
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+2x(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡2x) \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =4(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡2x)-4x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2x)\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
4(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡2x)-4x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+4x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2x)=8\operatorname{cos}⁡2x-\operatorname{sin}⁡2x
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
-4\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡2x+4\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡2x=8\operatorname{cos}⁡2x-\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}4\beta =8\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡2x) \\ -4\alpha =-1\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =\frac{1}{4}$ and $\beta =2.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=x(\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2x).
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+x(\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2x).
$$

Find the general solutionto the problem

$$
{y}^{″}+16y=16\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+8\operatorname{sin}⁡4x.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
{y}^{″}+16y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-16\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =\pm 4\text{i}$, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡4x.
$$

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The particular solution of the inhomogeneous equation cannot be of the form $\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡4x$ because this is already included in the complementary function. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡4x),
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & =(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡4x)+4x(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡4x) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & =8(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡4x)+16x(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡4x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡4x).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
8(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡4x)+16x(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡4x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡4x)+16x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡4x)\,=16\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+8\operatorname{sin}⁡4x
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
-8\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡4x+8\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡4x=16\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+8\operatorname{sin}⁡4x.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}8\beta =16\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡4x) \\ -8\alpha =8\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡4x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-1$ and $\beta =2.$ Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=x(-\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+2\operatorname{sin}⁡4x)=-x\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+2x\operatorname{sin}⁡4x
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡4x-x\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+2x\operatorname{sin}⁡4x.
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{1}{2}$, $\beta =0.$
Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-\frac{1}{2}x\operatorname{cos}⁡4x.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}=P\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡4x-\frac{1}{2}x\operatorname{cos}⁡4x.
$$

questions.problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+25y=-20\operatorname{cos}⁡5x-10\operatorname{sin}⁡5x
$$

has the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡5x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡5x,$ find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
questions.worked_solution:
The particular solution of the inhomogeneous equation cannot be of the form $\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡5x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡5x$ because this is already included in the complementary function. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡5x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡5x),
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡5x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡5x)+5x(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡5x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡5x) \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =10(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡5x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡5x)-25x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡5x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡5x)\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
10(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡5x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡5x)-25x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡5x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡5x)+25x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡5x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡5x)=-20\operatorname{cos}⁡5x-10\operatorname{sin}⁡5x
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
-10\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡5x+10\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡5x=-20\operatorname{cos}⁡5x-10\operatorname{sin}⁡5x.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}10\beta =-20\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡5x) \\ -10\alpha =-10\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡5x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =1$ and $\beta =-2.$ Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=x\operatorname{cos}⁡5x-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡5x.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
{y}^{″}+2{y}^{′}+y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +1 & =0 \\ {(\lambda +1)}^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =-1$ is a repeated root, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}
$$

We now need to find the particular solution${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $-25\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.$ Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2x,
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡2x+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡2x \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =-4\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2x-4\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2x\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
(-4\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2x-4\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+2(-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡2x+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡2x)+(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2x)=-25\operatorname{sin}⁡2x
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
(-3\alpha +4\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+(-4\alpha -3\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡2x=-25\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}-3\alpha +4\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡2x) \\ -4\alpha -3\beta =-25\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =4$ and $\beta =3.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+3\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}+4\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+3\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.
$$

Now let us find constants $A$ and $B.$ 

Substituting $y(0)=4$ into the general solution gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}A+4 & =4 \\ A & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}:$

$$
{y}^{′}=-A{e}^{-x}+B{e}^{-x}-Bx{e}^{-x}-8\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+6\operatorname{cos}⁡2x
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ into the above gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}-A+B+6 & =0 \\ B & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $A=0,B=-6.$

So, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=-6x{e}^{-x}+4\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+3\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.
$$

questions.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4y=-25\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

has the general solution

$$
y(x)=A{e}^{2x}+Bx{e}^{2x}+4\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3\operatorname{cos}⁡x,
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4y=-25\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,y(0)=-3,\,{y}^{′}(0)=5.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We find the constants $A$ and $B$ by substituting the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(0)=-3$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-3 & =A{e}^{2(0)}+B(0){e}^{2(0)}+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(0) \\ -3 & =A-3 \\ A & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $y$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=2A{e}^{2x}+2Bx{e}^{2x}+B{e}^{2x}+4\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=5$ into the derivative gives

$$
\begin{aligned}5 & =2A{e}^{2(0)}+2B(0){e}^{2(0)}+B{e}^{2(0)}+4\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(0) \\ 5 & =2A+B+4 \\ 5 & =2(0)+B+4 \\ B & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $A=0$ and $B=1,$ we have the following solution to the initial value problem:

$$
y=x{e}^{2x}+4\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
{y}^{″}+9y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+9 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-9\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =\pm 3\text{i},$ and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=P\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡3x.
$$

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The particular solution of the inhomogeneous equation cannot be of the form $\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3x$ because this is already included in the complementary function. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3x),
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3x)+3x(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡3x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡3x) \\ {y}^{″} & =6(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡3x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡3x)+9x(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3x).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
6(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡3x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡3x)+9x(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3x)+9x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3x)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡3x-12\operatorname{sin}⁡3x
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
-6\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡3x+6\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡3x=6\operatorname{cos}⁡3x-12\operatorname{sin}⁡3x.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}6\beta =6\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡3x) \\ -6\alpha =-12\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡3x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =2,\beta =1.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=x(2\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\operatorname{sin}⁡3x).
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=P\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡3x+x(2\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\operatorname{sin}⁡3x).
$$

Now let us find constants $P$ and $Q.$ 

Substituting $y(0)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$
P=2.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=5.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
{y}^{′}=-3P\operatorname{sin}⁡3x+3Q\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\operatorname{sin}⁡3x)+x(-6\operatorname{sin}⁡3x+3\operatorname{cos}⁡3x)
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=5$ into the above gives

$$
3Q+2=5.
$$

Therefore, $P=2,Q=1.$

So, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=2\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\operatorname{sin}⁡3x+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+x\operatorname{sin}⁡3x.
$$

First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
{y}^{″}+4{y}^{′}-5y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda -5 & =0 \\ (\lambda +5)(\lambda -1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =-5$ or $\lambda =1$, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-5x}+B{e}^{x}.
$$

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $\operatorname{cos}⁡3x-4\operatorname{sin}⁡3x.$ Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3x,
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡3x+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡3x \\ {y}^{″} & =-9\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3x-9\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3x.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
-9\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3x-9\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3x+4(-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡3x+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡3x)-5(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡3x-4\operatorname{sin}⁡3x
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives:

$$
(-14\alpha +12\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+(-14\beta -12\alpha )\operatorname{sin}⁡3x=\operatorname{cos}⁡3x-4\operatorname{sin}⁡3x
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}-14\alpha +12\beta =1\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡3x) \\ -14\beta -12\alpha =-4\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡3x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =\frac{1}{10},\beta =\frac{1}{5}.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡3x.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{-5x}+B{e}^{x}+\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡3x.
$$

Now let us find constants $A$ and $B.$ 

Substituting $y(0)=-\frac{2}{5}$ into the general solution gives

$$
A+B=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=\frac{1}{10}.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
{y}^{′}=-5A{e}^{-5x}+B{e}^{x}-\frac{3}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡3x+\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡3x
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=\frac{1}{10}$ into the above gives

$$
-5A+B=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations for $A$ and $B$:

$$
{\begin{aligned}A+B=-\frac{1}{2} \\ -5A+B=-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=0,$ $B=-\frac{1}{2}.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x}+\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡3x.
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & =A{e}^{-2(0)}+B(0){e}^{-2(0)}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2(0) \\ -1 & =A-2 \\ A & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

Finally, since $A=1$ and $B=0,$ we have the following solution to the initial value problem:

$$
y={e}^{-2x}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2} + 4y = 4\sin 2x.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the complementary solution by solving the associated homogeneous ODE. The characteristic equation has roots $\lambda = \pm 2 \textrm{i},$ so the complementary solution is 

$$
y_c = A\cos{2x} + B \sin{2x}.
$$

We now need to find the particular solution $y_p(x).$

Second, we find a particular solution of the inhomogeneous ODE. We see that the right-hand side is $4 \sin 2x,$ and $\sin 2x$ is a term in the complementary solution. So, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
y_p = x (\alpha \cos{2x} + \beta \sin{2x}),
$$

where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of $y_p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+2x(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡2x), \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =4(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡2x)+4x(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2x).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha$ and $\beta,$ we substitute the derivatives into the original ODE and get

$$
\begin{aligned}4(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡2x)+4x(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+4x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2x) & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡2x \\ -4\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡2x+4\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡2x & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}4\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡2x) \\ -4\alpha =4\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha = -1$ and $\beta = 0.$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
y_p(x) = -x \cos{2x},
$$

and the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={y}_{c}+{y}_{p} \\  & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡2x-x\operatorname{cos}⁡2x.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2} + 4y = 4\sin 2x
$$

has the general solution

$$
y(x) = A \cos{2x} + B \sin{2x} - x \cos{2x},
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2} + 4y = 4\sin 2x, \qquad y(0) = 2 , \ \ y'(0) = -3.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We find the constants $A$ and $B$ by substituting the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(0)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡0+B\operatorname{sin}⁡0-0\operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\ 2 & =A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $y$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-2A\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+2B\operatorname{cos}⁡2x-(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡2x) \\  & =-2A\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+2B\operatorname{cos}⁡2x-\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+2x\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y'(0)=-3$ into the derivative gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-3 & =-2A\operatorname{sin}⁡0+2B\operatorname{cos}⁡0-\operatorname{cos}⁡0+2(0)\operatorname{sin}⁡0 \\ -3 & =2B-1 \\ -2 & =2B \\ -1 & =B.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $A=2$ and $B=-1,$ we have the following solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}y=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x-\operatorname{sin}⁡2x-x\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\end{aligned}
$$
